questions.q: What is the psalmist asking the Shepherd of Israel to do?
questions.a: The psalmist is asking him to pay attention and to reveal his glory to them.

questions.q: What is the psalmist asking the Shepherd of Israel to do in the sight of the tribes of Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh?
questions.a: He is asking the Shepherd of Israel to stir up his power and come and save them.

questions.q: What is the psalmist asking God to do?
questions.a: He is asking God to restore their strength, regard them favorably, and save them.

questions.q: What was Yahweh’s response when his people prayed?
questions.a: He was angry at his people so when they prayed, he did not answer.

questions.q: What has Yahweh caused them to experience?
questions.a: He has caused them to experience punishment through constant sorrow just as if he gave them tears for their food and drink.

questions.q: What are Israel’s neighbors and enemies doing to them?
questions.a: The nations are hostile to them, and their enemies mock and make fun of them.

questions.q: What did God do with the people that he brought out of Egypt?
questions.a: He drove out nations before them and allowed his people to settle in it like a vine that was transplanted from one place to another.

questions.q: What did God do to prepare for his people to move into the land?
questions.a: God removed the foreign nations just as a farmer clears land for a new plant.

questions.q: What does the psalmist say about the people of God?
questions.a: He says they became so numerous it was like a vine that covered the mountains, and whose branches were like the great cedars.

questions.q: How far did the people’s influence extend?
questions.a: They controlled territory as far as the sea in the west and the Euphrates River in the east.

questions.q: What has God allowed to happen?
questions.a: The land has been conquered and its protective walls broken down so that those who pass by can take whatever they want.

questions.q: What will the enemies do to the country?
questions.a: They will destroy it until it is as if wild boars had chewed up a vine and other wild animals ate what was left.

questions.q: What does the psalmist ask the God of armies to do for his people?
questions.a: He asks the God of armies to turn around and look down from heaven and see and respond to his people who are like a vine that he had planted.

questions.q: Who planted the people and made them grown strong in the land?
questions.a: The right hand of the God of armies planted the people and caused them to become strong.

questions.q: What is happening to the people?
questions.a: Their enemies are destroying them as if someone had cut down and burned a vine.

questions.q: What does the psalmist want God to do for his own people?
questions.a: The psalmist wants God to help them and to restore their power.

questions.q: What will the people do if God revives them?
questions.a: They will worship him and not turn back to worship other gods.

questions.q: What will happen if Yahweh, the God of armies, restores the people?
questions.a: If Yahweh restores them, they will be saved.

commentary.text: The psalmist complains of the miseries of the church.
Its former prosperity and present desolation.

Verses 1–7 He that dwelleth upon the mercy-seat, is the good Shepherd of his people. But we can neither expect the comfort of his love, nor the protection of his arm, unless we partake of his converting grace. If he is really angry at the prayers of his people, it is because, although they pray, their ends are not right, or there is some secret sin indulged in them, or he will try their patience and perseverance in prayer. When God is displeased with his people, we must expect to see them in tears, and their enemies in triumph. There is no salvation but from God's favour; there is no conversion to God but by his own grace.

The church is represented as a vine and a vineyard. The root of this vine is Christ, the branches are believers. The church is like a vine, needing support, but spreading and fruitful. If a vine do not bring forth fruit, no tree is so worthless. And are not we planted as in a well-cultivated garden, with every means of being fruitful in works of righteousness? But the useless leaves of profession, and the empty boughs of notions and forms, abound far more than real piety. It was wasted and ruined. There was a good reason for this change in God's way toward them. And it is well or ill with us, according as we are under God's smiles or frowns. When we consider the state of the purest part of the visible church, we cannot wonder that it is visited with sharp corrections. They request that God would help the vine. Lord, it is formed by thyself, and for thyself, therefore it may, with humble confidence, be committed to thyself.

The Messiah, the Protector and Saviour of the church, is the Man of God's right hand; he is the Arm of the Lord, for all power is given to him. In him is our strength, by which we are enabled to persevere to the end. The vine, therefore, cannot be ruined, nor can any fruitful branch perish; but the unfruitful will be cut off and cast into the fire. The end of our redemption is, that we should serve Him who hath redeemed us, and not go back to our old sins.
